papers.title: Corrupted by Reasoning: Reasoning Language Models Become Free-Riders in Public Goods Games
papers.how_tested: 7 LLM agents play a 15-round public goods game with per-round choice between a sanctioning institution (members may pay 1 token to reward a peer +1 or punish a peer -3) and a sanction-free institution; enforcement choices and punish/reward ratios are measured against human data.
papers.finding: Traditional LLMs mostly join the sanctioning institution and sustain high contributions but enforce almost entirely through rewards (punish/reward ratio 0.00-0.50 vs 1.66 for humans); reasoning models (o1/o3) tend to opt out and free-ride.

papers.title: Cultural Evolution of Cooperation among LLM Agents
papers.how_tested: Generations of LLM agents play an iterated Donor Game with cultural transmission of strategies; one condition adds a costly punishment option.
papers.finding: Claude 3.5 Sonnet uses costly punishment to reach higher scores, whereas Gemini 1.5 Flash and GPT-4o fail to benefit from it.

papers.title: The Role of Social Learning and Collective Norm Formation in Fostering Cooperation in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
papers.how_tested: LLM agents harvest a common-pool resource; agents monitor random peers and may punish norm violators at cost gamma to impose penalty beta; punishment is switched off mid-run and its strength varied.
papers.finding: Punishment sustains cooperation; when it is removed at timestep 15 cooperation collapses and the resource depletes faster; stronger punishment generally improves survival at moderate growth rates.

papers.title: Evolution of Cooperation in LLM-Agent Societies: A Preliminary Study Using Different Punishment Strategies
papers.how_tested: LLM agents assigned Boyd-Richerson strategy types (e.g., Cooperator-Punishers, Moralists, Reluctant Cooperators) play a Diner's Dilemma with explicit punishment and pairwise-imitation strategy adoption.
papers.finding: Explicit punishment drives norm emergence; Reluctant Cooperators defect initially but switch to cooperation after being punished.

papers.title: Investigating Prosocial Behavior Theory in LLM Agents under Policy-Induced Inequities
papers.how_tested: Multiple LLM agents in a simulated social network face policy-induced inequities; third-party punishment is measured while inequity magnitude and enforcement cost are varied.
papers.finding: Agents' third-party punishment responds to inequity magnitude and enforcement cost, and structural inequities suppress prosocial behavior and spread norm erosion.

papers.title: Formal Mechanisms for Market Stability in Self-Interested Agent Societies: A Marketplace Simulation Study
papers.authors: Eugene Ng Yi Sheng et al.
papers.how_tested: 18 DeepSeek-V3 agents trade over 200 rounds under eight conditions, including bilateral contracts with a 6-utility breach penalty, an oracle issuing escalating fines (-2/-4/-6) then suspension, peer costly sanctions (1 utility to inflict 3), and a judicial complaint system with 5-utility penalties.
papers.finding: Penalty-based mechanisms underperform: costly sanctions rank last because agents free-ride on others' punishment, contracting has a 21.3% breach rate and cuts trade volume to a third, oracle fines give the lowest inequality but 17% less welfare than mediation.

papers.title: Institutional AI: Governing LLM Collusion in Multi-Agent Cournot Markets via Public Governance Graphs
papers.how_tested: LLM firms in a repeated Cournot market under three regimes (ungoverned, prompt-only prohibition, governance graph enforced by an oracle/controller with warnings, tiered fines of 35/75/100% of round profit, and suspension); collusion severity measured over 90 runs per condition.
papers.finding: Enforced fines/suspension cut mean collusion tier from 3.1 to 1.8 (d=1.28) and severe collusion from 50% to 5.6%; the prompt-only rule has negligible effect.

papers.title: Commitment To Cooperation With Self-Negotiated Contracts
papers.how_tested: LLM agents negotiate contracts (programmatic or natural-language, judge-enforced) in a spatial-temporal bargaining game; contracts specify automatically executed conditional transfers, and an agent unable to honor a transfer gets a score of 0.
papers.finding: Self-negotiated contracts improve cooperation beyond ordinary trading; defection rates vary widely (0.04-0.94) by model and contract type. No explicit penalty clauses, so this is partial evidence for P03-04.

papers.title: CoopEval: Benchmarking Cooperation-Sustaining Mechanisms and LLM Agents in Social Dilemmas
papers.how_tested: Benchmarks LLM agent pairs in social dilemmas under repetition, reputation, third-party mediation, and contract agreements (outcome-conditional payments between players).
papers.finding: Contracting and mediation are the most effective mechanisms for cooperation among capable LLMs; contracts are outcome-conditional payments rather than breach penalties, so this is partial evidence for P03-04.

papers.title: Cooperate or Collapse: Emergence of Sustainable Cooperation in a Society of LLM Agents
papers.how_tested: LLM agents share a regenerating common-pool resource (GovSim) and communicate; utterances are coded with a dialogue taxonomy that includes a 'Punishment' category. No mechanical fines or sanctions exist.
papers.finding: Sanctioning shows up only as conversational pressure (relational utterances are about 1%); universalization reasoning and communication drive sustainability. Counts as measured, not manipulated, verbal disapproval.

papers.title: Everyone Contributes! Incentivizing Strategic Cooperation in Multi-LLM Systems via Sequential Public Goods Games
papers.how_tested: Multi-LLM ensembles are trained with RL in a sequential public goods game whose public-goods reward is redesigned so that effortful contribution is the unique subgame-perfect equilibrium.
papers.finding: The redesigned reward removes free-riding and the trained ensembles beat single-agent and CoT baselines on reasoning, math, and code tasks. This is a training-reward redesign on a collaborative task, not a subsidy between agents, so partial.

papers.title: Investigating the Impact of Direct Punishment on the Emergence of Cooperation in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Systems
papers.venue: Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems 39, article 19 (2025)
papers.how_tested: MARL populations in social dilemmas with direct punishment, third-party punishment, partner selection and reputation, alone and combined.
papers.finding: Direct punishment supports cooperation, and its effect depends on how it combines with third-party punishment, partner selection and reputation.

papers.title: A learning agent that acquires social norms from public sanctions in decentralized multi-agent settings
papers.how_tested: Decentralized RL agents see all public sanctioning events; the architecture includes a classifier of approved/disapproved behavior and a motivation to punish in step with the group.
papers.finding: Agents acquire beneficial sanctioning norms that reduce free-riding and raise per-agent returns.

papers.title: Spurious normativity enhances learning of compliance and enforcement behavior in artificial agents
papers.how_tested: MARL agents in a foraging environment learn to punish peers who eat taboo berries; an extra 'silly rule' taboo on a harmless berry is added as a manipulation.
papers.finding: Peer punishment helps agents avoid poisonous berries, and the silly rule further improves returns by giving agents more practice at enforcement.

papers.title: Adaptive Punishment for Cooperation in Mixed-Motive Games
papers.how_tested: MARL agents in sequential social dilemmas and iterated public goods games use a learned punishment policy (APC) that sets punishment probability and severity based on estimated defection severity.
papers.finding: APC cuts costly, ineffective punishment and raises cooperation above baseline punishment schemes.

papers.title: LOPT: Learning Optimal Pigovian Tax in Sequential Social Dilemmas
papers.venue: arXiv (a NeurIPS 2025 proceedings version appears in search results)
papers.how_tested: A central tax-planner agent learns Pigovian tax and allowance (subsidy) rates that reshape the rewards of self-interested MARL agents in Escape Room and Cleanup.
papers.finding: Learned tax/subsidy reward shaping gives higher social welfare than existing methods in both environments.

papers.title: Adaptive Mechanism Design: Learning to Promote Cooperation
papers.how_tested: An external planning agent learns to hand out extra rewards and punishments to independent learners in matrix social dilemmas, anticipating their parameter updates.
papers.finding: Learners reach high-welfare cooperation; the planner learns that punishing defection is cheaper than rewarding cooperation, and the incentives it has to pay fall toward zero over time.

papers.title: The AI Economist: Taxation policy design via two-level deep multiagent reinforcement learning
papers.how_tested: A planner learns tax schedules with redistribution while a population of RL economic agents co-adapts (two-level deep RL).
papers.finding: Learned tax policies improve the equality-productivity trade-off over baselines despite tax-gaming. The setting is an economy rather than a social dilemma, so partial for P04-02.

papers.title: Learning to Incentivize Other Learning Agents
papers.how_tested: Each RL agent learns an incentive function to give rewards directly to other agents, accounting for its effect on their learning, in social dilemmas (e.g., Escape Room, Cleanup).
papers.finding: Learned peer incentives beat standard RL and often reach a near-optimal division of labor. This is peer-to-peer reward, not a central subsidy.

papers.title: Gifting in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (Student Abstract)
papers.how_tested: RL agents in a Harvest common-pool resource environment get a gifting action that transfers reward to other agents.
papers.finding: Gifting can greatly improve learning progress in the resource-appropriation setting (preliminary student abstract).

papers.title: Formal Contracts Mitigate Social Dilemmas in Multi-Agent RL
papers.venue: arXiv; AAMAS 2023 as 'Get It in Writing: Formal Contracts Mitigate Social Dilemmas in Multi-Agent RL'
papers.how_tested: Markov games are augmented so agents can voluntarily agree to binding, pre-specified conditional reward transfers (MOCA training), tested on static games, traffic, pollution and common-pool resource domains.
papers.finding: With a rich enough contract space all subgame-perfect equilibria are socially optimal, and contracting raises welfare empirically. Transfers can act as pre-agreed penalties but are not framed as breach penalties, so partial.

papers.title: Resolving social dilemmas with minimal reward transfer
papers.how_tested: Defines a 'general self-interest level' and computes minimal reward-transfer structures that make the social optimum dominant in multi-player social dilemmas.
papers.finding: Minimal reward redistribution can align individual and group incentives; the work is mostly analytical, so partial.

papers.title: MRL-PoS: A Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning based Proof of Stake Consensus Algorithm for Blockchain
papers.how_tested: A PoS consensus design in which MARL agents (nodes) receive rewards and penalties to push out malicious validators and reward honest ones.
papers.finding: The abstract reports that the reward/penalty system removes malicious nodes. It is a blockchain security design, not a cooperation study, and does not report stake-slashing manipulation in detail, so partial.

mechanism_updates.seed_claims_checked: GovSim auto-deduction: mischaracterized. GovSim has no fines or automatic deductions; resource collapse is the only automatic consequence.

mechanism_updates.marl_evidence: haupt2022contracts (binding conditional reward transfers that can encode penalties).
mechanism_updates.seed_claims_checked: Seed says untested; moved to tested.

mechanism_updates.seed_claims_checked: SanctSim 'subsidies as primary enforcement tool': mischaracterized. SanctSim's rewards are peer-to-peer (cost 1, +1 to the target), not Pigouvian subsidies from a planner. The underlying finding (LLMs enforce mainly through rewards) holds.

mechanism_updates.marl_evidence: islam2023mrlpos (honest-node rewards in a MARL PoS design; not a cooperation experiment).

mechanism_updates.llm_evidence: Seed cites Kolt 2024 as discussion; this slice did not re-verify it. No LLM multi-agent test of defaults or nudges found.
mechanism_updates.seed_claims_checked: Kolt 2024: not checked in this slice (no search run); 'not tested' is consistent with what was found.

mechanism_updates.llm_evidence: guzman2025reasoning (both reward and punishment available; LLMs prefer rewards, humans prefer punishment at a 1.66 ratio).
mechanism_updates.marl_evidence: baumann2018adaptive (planner can reward or punish; learns that punishing defection is cheaper). Not a choice made by the peer agents themselves.
mechanism_updates.seed_claims_checked: SanctSim: confirmed. Human ratio 1.66 confirmed. LLM 0.00-0.50 confirmed for traditional LLMs; the seed's 0.88 upper bound (presumably reasoning models) was not seen on the page. The seed's 'o1 free-ride' claim fits the reported opt-out of the sanctioning institution.

mechanism_updates.llm_evidence: No LLM study where one member's defection penalizes the whole group. SanctSim sanction costs are borne individually.
mechanism_updates.marl_evidence: No MARL study found. arXiv 2109.05634 'Evolution of cooperation with joint liability' is evolutionary game theory, not learning agents; excluded.
mechanism_updates.seed_claims_checked: SanctSim 'shared-cost enforcement among members': mischaracterized. The paper states each sanctioner pays from a personal 20-token endowment with no cost-sharing and no group penalty.

notes: 1) Codebook gap: peer-to-peer monetary reward (SanctSim rewards, LIO, gifting) has no clean home in P04. P04-01 is praise/status and P04-02 is a central Pigouvian subsidy. Consider adding a 'peer reward / gifting' mechanism under primitive 4; for now peer-reward MARL papers are mapped to P04-02 as partial. 2) Three seed claims are mischaracterized: GovSim has no auto-deduction (P03-03); SanctSim rewards are not subsidies (P04-02) or praise (P04-01); SanctSim has no shared/collective cost (P07-01). 3) Collective liability (P07-01..03) is untested in both tracks. The only joint-liability hit (arXiv 2109.05634) is evolutionary game theory and was excluded. 4) Titles and venues to verify: zhou2025prosocial (arXiv v1 was titled 'Simulating Prosocial Behavior and Social Contagion in LLM Agents under Institutional Interventions'; the current abs page gives the title used here and AAAI 2026); hua2023lopt venue (a NeurIPS 2025 PDF appears in search, the arXiv page does not say); haupt2022contracts (the AAMAS 2023 version has a different title and possibly a different author order); islam2023mrlpos (the IEEE venue was not confirmed on the page). 5) Author strings: vinitsky2023sanctions, koster2022spurious and zheng2022aieconomist were taken from search snippets (publisher pages blocked or not opened); the arXiv or DOI pages should be checked. Syrnikov first name was not shown. 6) Excluded: Lee et al. 2025 arXiv 2507.04543 (evolutionary spatial PGG, not learning agents); Horibe et al. 2026 arXiv 2608.04507 (reward/punishment emerge as donation discrimination, which is reputation, primitive 5); Kumar et al. 2026 arXiv 2605.26448 (no sanction mechanism); Borah 2026 arXiv 2605.29062 (power asymmetry, no sanctions in the abstract); LToS NeurIPS 2022 (fully cooperative, not a dilemma). 7) Not chased for lack of budget: ALIGN gossip paper (ICML 2026, possibly reputation-based punishment); 'The Politician, the Liar, and the Obedient Worker' arXiv 2608.09574; IQ-Flow arXiv 2302.14604 and meta-gradient incentive design arXiv 2112.10859 (likely more MARL P04-02 evidence). 8) Screening counts are approximate: the number of results each web search returned, not a full database hit count.
